# Introduction 

Willow (*Lagopus lagopus*) and Rock Ptarmigan (*Lagopus muta*) are primary prey sources for the Gyrfalcon, a declining Arctic raptor species. For this research project, I aim to estimate annual ptarmigan abundance from data collected by the Peregrine Fund to support PhD student Michael Henderson's research linking adult survival of Gyrfalcons to ptarmigan numbers in Alaska along the Seward Peninsula.

## Research Question

How has ptarmigan abundance changed in the Seward Peninsula of Alaska over the last 10 years?

# Data

Since 2016, the Peregrine Fund has conducted annual distance sampling surveys along 10 mi road transects in the Seward Peninsula of Alaska. There are 15 transects, each surveyed 1-2x yearly. Surveys were completed by two observers scanning for ptarmigan in a vehicle around May each year from sunrise to noon, when ptarmigans are most active. When ptarmigan were spotted, observers tally birds and record distance to the bird with rangefinders. Data from 2016-2026 was cleaned and combined into one csv by Kara Beer. The first rows of the dataset and its dimensions are shown here:

```{r pulldata, echo = FALSE}
# set path to where you can access your data #
# Note that the path will be different for your.#
datapath <- datadir <- paste( getwd(), "/Data/", sep = "" )
# load ptarmigan raw detection data
detdf <- read.csv( file = paste( datadir, "2026-07-23_all_prey_data.csv", sep = ""),
                   header = TRUE )
#view
head( detdf ); dim( detdf )
```


## Cleaning

First, I removed all observations that are not of Rock or Willow Ptarmigan.
```{r cleannonptarm, include = FALSE}

#database has observations that are not ptarmigan. view all the species in the species column
unique(detdf$species)

#new dataframe with only relevant columns and only for ptarmigan obs.
ptarmdetdf <- detdf %>% 
  dplyr::select(year, round, transect, observer1, observer2, species, males, females, cluster_size, distance) %>% #select relevant columns (cluster_size = ptarmigan count),
  dplyr::filter(., species == "WIPT" | species == "ROPT" )  #filter out rows that are not willow and rock ptarmigan counts

#view
head(ptarmdetdf); dim(ptarmdetdf)

```
This removed `r nrow( detdf ) - nrow(ptarmdetdf)` observations.

In my initial data exploration, I discovered that the data in the distance row was character class instead of numeric class due to the inclusion of values such as "<100," ">1200," and "U". There were also one negative distance recorded. My next cleaning step is to turn the column into numeric values and filter out the NAs converted from the greater than, less than values, and U values.

```{r cleandistance, include = FALSE}

# First, check class of distance column
sapply(ptarmdetdf$distance, class)
# all character

#convert to numeric
ptarmdetdf$distance <- as.numeric(ptarmdetdf$distance)

#check again to make sure
sapply(ptarmdetdf$distance, class)
#all numeric

#drop all rows with NAs and the negative numbers
cleandetdf <- ptarmdetdf %>%
  drop_na(.,"distance") %>%
  subset(., distance >= 0)

#check for NAs
sum(is.na(cleandetdf$distance))
#0 NAs

#view
head(cleandetdf); dim(cleandetdf)

```

This cleaning step removed `r nrow( ptarmdetdf ) - nrow(cleandetdf)` rows.

There are pretty wide disparities between species and sex, so it may be best to run 4 separate models.

## Visualization

Key to distance sampling models is fitting distance sampling curves to detection of ptarmigan by distance. I will create histograms of distance to ptarmigan for each observer pair by year for each round of surveys to look for any potential biases (are some pairs better at looking for ptarmigan than others? Are observers better at finding ptarmigan close to the road than further from the road?). This visualization also will tell us what kind of distance curves we should use.

First, I visualized the general histogram of all distances ptarmigans are detected at and by species. To run the model specified in Royle and Kery's (2016) book chapter Modeling Abundance Using Hierarchical Distance Sampling in Applied Hierarchical Modeling in Ecology, distances will need to be binned into classes. Royle and Kery advises that bin widths be <10% of the max distance. The highest distance recorded for Willow Ptarmigan is `r max(wipt$distance)` m, and 10% of which is `r max(wipt$distance)/10` m. The highest distance recorded for Rock Ptarmigan is `r max(ropt$distance)` m, and 10% of which is `r max(ropt$distance)/10` m. Thus, bins of 50 m should suffice. There should be no need to truncate distances as long as distances are binned.

```{r allhist, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}

#plot histogram of distances grouped by species
ggplot( cleandetdf, aes(x = distance, fill = species)) +
  theme_classic() +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) #bin 50 because I'm planning to bin final data by 50 m

```

To start the process of visualizing data by round and observer pair, I first added a column to my dataframe with each unique pair of observers.

```{r obspair, include = FALSE}

#make a column with each unique pair of observers
cleandetdf$obsv_pair <- apply(cleandetdf[, c("observer1", "observer2")], 1, function(x) {
   last <- word(x, -1)
   tolower(paste(sort(last), collapse = "-"))
 })

#view
cleandetdf$obsv_pair

#what are the unique observer pairs?
unique(cleandetdf$obsv_pair)

#check for NAs just in case
sum(is.na(cleandetdf$obsv_pair))
  
```
The unique observer pairs are: `r unique(cleandetdf$obsv_pair)`

So far, distance data for both species fits a half normal distribution for the distance curve. Next, I create two different dataframes for each of the two rounds of surveys to eventually compare possible data discrepancies in round 1 vs 2.

```{r rounds, include = FALSE}
#view

```
There are `r nrow(det1)` observations in all round 1 surveys and `r nrow(det2)` observations in all round 2 surveys.

### Histograms by Survey Round

Here are histograms for each round:
```{r roundshist, echo = FALSE}
#plot histogram of distances for each round grouped by species
ggplot( det1, aes(x = distance, fill = species)) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs( title = "Round 1" ) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50)

ggplot( det2, aes(x = distance, fill = species)) +
  theme_classic() +
  labs( title = "Round 2" ) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) 
```

Round 1 has more data than round 2, but both fit the half normal distribution shape well, and each distance bin has proportionally about the same distance count in each round. From this visualization, I would consider only using round 1 data for the final model because it's similar enough to round 2 but has more data.

### Round 1 Histograms by Observer Pair

Here are the histograms for round 1 of surveys for each observer pair by year to see if there are data from any pairs that should be excluded.

```{r round1hist, echo = FALSE, warning = FALSE, message = FALSE}

#create an object that stores all unique observer pairs
pairs1 <- c(unique(det1$obsv_pair))
#view
pairs1

#for loop to create histograms of distance by observer pair/year and survey (1st or 2nd)
for( p in 1:length(pairs1) ){
  # create an object with the ggplot so that you can display it 
  # in a loop 
  a <- ggplot( subset(det1, obsv_pair %in% pairs1[p]), aes(x = distance, fill = species) ) + #data subsetted to observer pair by year. plot distance and color code by species.
    theme_bw( base_size = 15 ) + #choose a preset theme
    labs( title = pairs1[p], subtitle = "Round 1" ) + #label graphs using our observer pairs
    geom_histogram(binwidth = 50) + #plot histogram
    facet_wrap(~year) #plot by survey 1 and 2
    #scale_x_discrete(breaks = scales::pretty_breaks(5))
  # display your plot object
  print( a )
}
```

INTERPRETATION

## Predictors

I will not be looking at covariates for detection or abundance for the class project to keep it simple. Observers did collect environmental covariates for each survey (eg temp, wind speed), so future analysis could include them in the detection submodel to determine whether or not they influenced detection. Factors like vegetation cover and landscape features (would obscure ptarmigan, especially further out) could also influence detection, so we could consider getting these covariate values from remote sensed data, but that might be too complicated for right now. Factors like gyrfalcon and other predator abundance and vegetation data (since adults are herbivorous) could influence abundance, but ptarmigan also naturally cycle in population numbers in some areas, which could include our study area. It might be best to not include a covariate model on abundance for now and first see how the numbers look year to year.

# Analysis

I will use the unmarked package distsamp function to run a hierarchical distance sampling model following Royle and Kery (2016). I may run 4 separate models (by species and sex). The general equation will be:


Abundance: N(s) ~ Poisson(Lambda(s)) where s = sites

Detection: (y(s1)...y(sH)) ~ Multinomial(N(s), pi(s)), where (y(s1)...y(sH)) are observations in each distance class h and pi(s) is a parameter describing multinomial cell probabilities (the probability an individual is both occurs and is in distance class h). 

Unlike conventional distance sample (CDS) models, hierarchical distance sampling (HDS) models account for spatial variation in abundance between sites, since Lambda(s) measures mean site-level abundance. Total abundance in the area can still be calculated, but HDS allows us to get at the reasons for spatial variation among sites if we so choose (i.e., it's more flexible). 

## Model Evaluation

I will assess model goodness-of-fit using the Pearson chi-square statistic as suggested by Mackenzie and Bailey (2004) using the AICmodavg package. I will be looking for a high p-value and low chi-squared values by year. Then, I will evaluate the model against a null model using the pseudo R^2 described by Nagelkerke (2004) using the model selection function in unmarked. I will be looking for pseudo r squared values close to 1.

## Visualize and Interpret Results

I will plot total abundance of ptarmigan in the Seward Peninsula over time (by year). If I run 4 models, there will be 4 such graphs.
